prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, enabling measurement of time at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks meet the test I apply to every candidate: an original invention, experimentally verified, with consequences beyond its own subfield. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and first strontium lattice clock are the origin of the idea, and Ye's group carried it to the 10^-18 regime. Many independent laboratories now reproduce and intercompare these clocks, so I can be 'absolutely sure' about the topic and about who did the original work. It is a tool that opens a door: tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and a path to redefining the second. The opening ballots show this is the broadest-supported candidate that also has a compact, two-name attribution, which a three-person ceiling makes valuable.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty relative to earlier precision-measurement prizes (frequency combs 2005, ion-trap control 2012). If the committee judges the lattice clock a refinement of those achievements rather than a distinct invention, the prize would look like honouring the best later experiment, which I have said we should not do. There is also a residual question whether Ye's contribution is the original idea or the later accuracy record, so the citation must be anchored on the invention and realization rather than on the record.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first and aberration-corrected electron optics fourth, valuing new measurement capabilities, while noting that Krivanek is the strongest missing name for B019 and that the 1986 electron microscope prize is a precedent.
responses.response: I agree on Krivanek, and I accept that this weakens the cleanliness of my own opening first choice. In STEM correction the lineage is not limited to Rose, Haider and Urban, and I cannot claim the historical record is settled within three names. A prize for the corrector would therefore risk crediting the wrong people, which I would not accept. With only two of eight members ranking B019, I defer and keep it as an alternative. I do agree with your reading of the lattice clock: the idea (Katori) and the realization (Ye) are separable and well verified.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the lattice clock first and attributes it cleanly to Katori with Ye as the leading realization, treating overlap with the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion prize as acknowledged but not decisive.
responses.response: I largely agree and this is why I move the lattice clock to my preferred configuration. I would add a procedural caution: the citation should name the lattice clock concept with magic-wavelength trapping and its realization, so the committee cannot be accused of rewarding the combs again. I would also like the committee to check the record on Lemonde and Boyd, and on the Ye group's contributions before Katori's in other implementations, since you and Johansson both raise them. I think the two credited names survive that check, but I would not state it as proven.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators first and magic-angle graphene second, valuing new quantum states of matter, and accepts the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp trio as clean despite the BHZ prediction lying outside the credit.
responses.response: I did not rank B008 in my opening and I should explain that. The experiment (Molenkamp, 2007) is verified and the theory is original, so I do not dispute its merit. My difficulty is attribution: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang predicted the specific HgTe system that Molenkamp measured, and the committee cannot call the credit clean while that prediction sits outside the three names. Zhang's death in 2018 narrows what is possible. I consider B008 a serious alternative and I would support it if colleagues in condensed matter can show the HgTe experiment is rightly credited to the Kane-Mele proposal alone.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first because it is an instrument-driven discovery of a new window, and treats Halzen, Karle and Spiering as a defensible set, with the allocation among founders unsettled.
responses.response: I share your weight on instrument-driven discoveries, which is why I ranked IceCube fourth. My hesitation is the one you name: the sources of most of the diffuse flux are unresolved and the AMANDA and Baikal pioneers are outside the credited names. A large collaboration also makes the 'who did the original work' question harder here than for the lattice clock. I would not block it, but I do not think the attribution is as secure as for the clock.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first and the lattice clock second, noting that circuit QED is distinct from the 2025 prize but close to it, and that he may need to consider recusal given his professional ties to that community.
responses.response: Your disclosure is appropriate, and I note you are also at Chalmers Physics, which I would flag on my side as well. On the substance, circuit QED is mature and important, but I think the committee should leave more distance after 2025, and Girvin's absence from the credited names is a real attribution gap. I take your support for the lattice clock as the common ground between us.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as distinct enough from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Whether contributions by other lattice-clock pioneers (for example Lemonde, Boyd, Takamoto) should alter the two-name credit.
Whether Krivanek and the STEM corrector lineage can be reconciled with a three-person B019 configuration, which determines if I can support it as a serious alternative.
Whether the BHZ prediction should be credited alongside Kane, Mele and Molenkamp for B008.
statement.conflict_note: My own field is transmission electron microscopy, so B019 (aberration-corrected electron optics) is in my direct research community and I would consider recusing from the vote on B019 if it advances. As IFSM President I have professional contact with the microscopy community, though my profile shows no personal tie to Rose, Urban or Haider. For the preferred B035 configuration no specific conflict is apparent from my profile. I note that Göran Johansson is a Chalmers Physics colleague, relevant only to his circuit QED ballot B004.
